title: Isandro and the Silence
premise: Lior Ishikawa, a translator whose childhood language is dissolving word by word, returns to their mother's coastal hometown for her funeral, where a stranger named Isandro greets mourners using a family name no one has spoken in forty years. Digging through old photographs and the mother's untranslated letters, Lior discovers Isandro was the brother erased from every family story—disowned after a betrayal that split loyalty from truth. As Lior's own memory of the mother frays, they must decide whether to preserve the comfortable silence or restore the brother to the record. The novel ends with Lior translating the mother's final letter aloud at a small gathering, forgiving Isandro and reclaiming both language and belonging.
about_author: Wendell Sterling is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent two decades listening to other people's truths before writing his own. He lives near the sea and writes about families, translation, and the words we lose on purpose.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Establishes Lior's rootless life in the city, translating contracts by day while childhood words slip away—one borrowed term at a time. A phone call announces the mother's death. Emotional beat: numb displacement, grief not yet landed.

chapters.title: Salt Road Home
chapters.summary: Lior travels to the coastal town of their childhood, noticing how little is remembered correctly—the streets renamed, the bakery gone. First-person memories arrive in the fading mother tongue. Beat: uneasy homecoming, the past half-recognizable.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: At the wake, a weathered stranger helps carry chairs and calls the family by an unfamiliar surname. Lior's aunt goes pale and ushers him out. Beat: first crack in the family's official story; curiosity sharpened into dread.

chapters.title: The Photograph with the Folded Corner
chapters.summary: Sorting the mother's belongings, Lior finds photos with one figure creased or cut away, and a locked tin box. Aunt Marisol warns them to leave the past buried. Beat: loyalty to the living pitted against hunger for truth.

chapters.title: Isandro
chapters.summary: Lior tracks the stranger to a boatyard. Isandro admits he is the mother's brother, disowned decades ago, and asks nothing except to attend the burial from the back row. Beat: reluctant sympathy; the enemy has a human face.

chapters.title: What the Sea Keeps
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV flashback: 1979, two siblings, a fishing debt, and the night he reported the father's smuggling to protect his sister—and was cast out for it. Beat: the betrayal reframed as sacrifice, though his account may be self-serving.

chapters.title: The Tin Box
chapters.summary: Lior picks the lock and finds the mother's letters, written in the dying language, addressed but never sent—to Isandro. Lior can barely read them. Beat: grief deepens as the mother's voice emerges posthumously, just out of reach.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Lior consults an elderly dictionary-keeper, Mrs. Okafor, who trades translations for stories. Each recovered word costs Lior a memory of the mother. Beat: the central bargain made explicit—language returns only as memory leaves.

chapters.title: Marisol's Version
chapters.summary: Aunt Marisol tells her truth: Isandro informed on the father, the father drowned fleeing, the family starved. Her grief is real and her certainty absolute. Beat: rising tension; two irreconcilable truths now stand side by side.

chapters.title: The Burial
chapters.summary: Isandro stands at the cemetery fence as agreed. When the priest stumbles over the eulogy, Lior impulsively invites him inside the gate. Half the family walks out. Beat: point of no return; Lior chooses truth over harmony.

chapters.title: Letters, Unsent
chapters.summary: With Mrs. Okafor's help, Lior translates the first letter: the mother wrote to Isandro every year on the drowning anniversary, never mailing any. Beat: devastating tenderness; the silence was the mother's, not the family's alone.

chapters.title: Cousins at the Door
chapters.summary: Angry relatives confront Lior, accusing them of desecrating the dead for a stranger's redemption. Lior's cousin Tomás reveals a detail that contradicts Marisol's timeline. Beat: family fractures widen; doubt spreads.

chapters.title: The Harbor Records
chapters.summary: Lior and Isandro search municipal archives for the coast guard log from the night of the storm. The page is missing—torn out deliberately. Beat: thriller-tinged escalation; someone in the family destroyed evidence.

chapters.title: What Lior Forgot
chapters.summary: A recovered word unlocks a suppressed memory: child-Lior saw the father alive after the supposed drowning date, boarding a night boat. Beat: vertigo; the foundation of everyone's grief may be false.

chapters.title: Marisol Breaks
chapters.summary: Confronted, Marisol confesses she tore the log page—not to protect the father's name, but because the mother asked her to, so the children would have a clean story to belong to. Beat: climax of revelation; the silence was an act of love.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: The final unsent letter, translated at last: the mother forgave Isandro years ago and begged him to come home; shame kept him circling for decades. Beat: emotional peak; forgiveness already exists, waiting to be delivered.

chapters.title: Night Boat
chapters.summary: Lior and Isandro visit the cove where the father actually departed—alive, choosing exile over arrest, abandoning them all. Isandro weeps for the first time. Beat: catharsis; the villain of the story was never Isandro.

chapters.title: The Family Table
chapters.summary: Lior hosts an uninvited dinner, reads the mother's letter aloud in the old language, and sets a place for Isandro. Some cousins stay, some leave forever. Beat: costly reconciliation; belonging offered without guarantee.

chapters.title: Translation
chapters.summary: Lior declines a lucrative contract abroad, realizing they cannot translate what they refuse to inhabit. They begin translating the mother's full correspondence instead. Beat: quiet resolution of the vocation thread; identity reclaimed through work.

chapters.title: Mrs. Okafor's Ledger
chapters.summary: Lior repays the dictionary-keeper with the story of everything learned, and discovers Mrs. Okafor kept her own silences. Beat: thematic echo; every keeper of memory chooses what to withhold.

chapters.title: The Name Restored
chapters.summary: The headstone is recut with the family's original surname, Isandro standing beside Lior as it's unveiled. Marisol comes, says nothing, and stays until the end. Beat: public restoration; grief given a shared shape.

chapters.title: Owner, Not Tenant
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, months later, staying in the mother's house, fluent enough now to dream in the old language. A new word arrives each morning like tide. Final beat: belonging chosen daily; the silence ended, the memory kept alive by telling.
